newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Menem asks Argentine unions to drop strike plans.
newsitem.headline: Menem asks Argentine unions to drop strike plans.

text.p: Argentine President Carlos Menem Friday told unions to resolve their grievances through negotiations and urged they scrap plans for a one-day general strike next month.
"I don't know what you'll get with a new stoppage," Menem said on FM News radio. "I am asking you to reconsider."

He told the CGT labor federation, which Thursday announced a 24-hour strike against the government's economic policies and police repression, to resume talks. "I have always invited you to dialogue," he said.

But CGT leader Rodolfo Daer told reporters late Thursday in announcing the strike plans that "the government's ears are deaf to the demands of workers." He also chastised businessmen whose "reactionary attitudes have caused the breakdown in three-way negotiations on labor reforms."
The one-day stoppage which the CGT said will take place sometime in May would be the fourth since August, including two called against the government's free market labor reforms.

The strike announcement capped the CGT's self-styled "Day of National Mourning" Thursday, during which workers walked off the job for one hour each shift to protest the death of a young woman in riots last weekend in a southern province.

Twenty-four-year-old Teresa Rodriguez died from a gunshot wound Saturday when striking teachers and local residents clashed with paramilitary forces in the towns of Cutral-Co and Plaza Huincul in Neuquen province.
Rodriguez, a mother of three, was a passer-by. Her death sparked a nationwide teachers strike last Monday and a massive rally in the capital against the use of force to quell social unrest.
Neuquen teachers, who had been on strike for a month against 20 percent pay cuts, struck a deal with provincial authorities this week to end the stoppage.

But a group of local residents has continued to block off access to national highway 2, where the pitched battle with police took place last Saturday, demanding a solution to the region's high unemployment. The privatization of oil giant YPF five years ago left thousands in the area jobless.
